brief.situation: 06:10 on the night-to-day round in a nursing home. You are the nurse aide. You open the door of room 12 and find Mrs. Lindqvist, 84, on the floor beside her bed.
handover: Care plan: high fall risk. Bed in the low position, call light within reach, nonslip socks, toileting help on the 06:00 round.
Care plan alert: on a blood thinner. Report any fall or bump to the nurse at once.
Mild memory loss; usually knows where she is. Full code.
The nurse is at the far end of the hall.
howItWorks: The clock runs in real time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Your actions are a nurse aide's: observe, ask, call, comfort, measure vital signs, report, write it down. The nurse assesses and decides; no medicines or orders.
While you wait for the nurse or the paramedics, Skip jumps ahead and logs it; she keeps changing at the same pace.
Early on you are asked to write what you would do. Then a debrief scores what you did.

source.note: The nurse reaches the room about 2 min after the call light and a shout. No published standard was found for this interval.
Leaving to find the nurse and coming back with her takes about 2 min. No published standard was found for this interval.
Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Left alone without being told to stay still, she tries to get up after about a minute.
Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Told to stay still and that help is coming, she waits about 2.5 min before trying.
If nobody calls, the nurse comes past on her 06:25 round.
The nurse's head-to-toe check on the floor takes about 3 min. No published standard was found for this interval.

Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. New drowsiness and repeated questions about 6 min after the nurse's assessment. FLAG: the timing of a change after a head injury varies from minutes to hours; this is chosen to fall inside the run.
Paramedics arrive about 20 min after the nurse calls 911. No published standard was found for this interval.
She asks to be helped up 45 s after you find her.
The written question opens 20 s in, before she asks to be helped up.

source.cite: Chippewa Valley Technical College, Nursing Assistant (Open RN, CC BY 4.0), 3.2 Emergency Situations
source.note: Notify the nurse as soon as you observe the situation: within 1 min of finding her (the expert path calls at about 10 s).
A change reported 3-10 min after it appears: partial.
She rates her right hip pain 7 out of 10.

ask.label: Ask her what happened and where it hurts
ask.why: You are out of the room.

then.log: "What happened? Where am I?" She asks again a minute later. Her eyes keep closing.
"I needed the bathroom and the floor was wet. My right hip hurts, about a 7. I think I hit my head on the nightstand. Just help me up, dear."

lookOver.label: Look her over without moving her
lookOver.why: You are out of the room.

effects.log: On her right side beside the bed, awake. Right leg looks shorter than the left and turned outward. Red bump on the right forehead. Skin tear on the right forearm, oozing a little. Bare feet, puddle of urine by the bed, call light clipped to the far rail, bed in the high position.

watch.label: Watch her: alertness, breathing, color
watch.why: You are out of the room.

then.log: Drowsier than 10 minutes ago: eyes closing, slow to answer, asking the same question again. Breathing steady, color unchanged.
Awake, answering, knows where she is. Breathing easily. Pale, a little cold to touch.

vitals.label: Take her vital signs (pulse, respirations, blood pressure, temperature)
vitals.why: You are out of the room.

effects.log: Without moving her: radial pulse {pulse}, respirations {resp}, blood pressure {sbp}/{dbp} on the left arm, temperature {tempD} C.

callLight.label: Press the call light and call out for the nurse (stay with her)
callLight.why: Help is already coming, or you are out of the room.

effects.log: You unclip the call light, press it and call out: "I need the nurse in room 12, resident on the floor." You stay with her.

leave.label: Leave the room to find the nurse

effects.log: You go out to look for the nurse. Mrs. Lindqvist is alone on the floor.

stayStill.label: Tell her to stay still: the nurse is coming and you are staying with her
stayStill.why: You are out of the room.

effects.log: "Please stay still, Mrs. Lindqvist. The nurse is coming to check you, and I'm right here."
Blanket over her without moving her. She says that's better.

pressure.label: Gloves on: gentle pressure on the skin tear with gauze

effects.log: Gloves on; clean gauze held gently on the forearm. The oozing slows.

helpUp.label: Help her up into the chair
helpUp.why: You are out of the room.

effects.log: As you lift, she screams and her right leg gives way. You lower her back to the floor.

report.label: Tell the nurse what you found
report.available: live and nurseHere and not reportedNurse and not nurseLeft
report.why: Once the nurse is in the room.

options.label: Found at 06:10 on her right side beside the bed; right leg shorter and turned out; bump on the right forehead; skin tear right forearm
She fell out of bed because she didn't use the call light

effects.log: You tell the nurse what you found.

reportVitals.label: Tell the nurse her vital signs

reportVitals.why: Take them first, with the nurse here.

tellChange.available: live and nurseLeft and not emsArrived
tellChange.why: The nurse is in the room or has not left yet.

then.log: "She's drowsier and keeps asking the same question." The nurse comes straight back, starts neuro checks and calls the paramedics and the provider with the change.
Nurse (on the phone): "Thanks. Keep watching her and tell me the moment anything changes."

options.label: 06:10 found on floor beside bed, right side, awake; her words; right leg shorter and turned out; forehead bump; skin tear; what you did and the times; vital signs; who you told
"Resident fell out of bed again, probably didn't use call light. Seemed OK. Nurse aware."

effects.log: Note written per facility policy; the nurse completes the incident report.

prevent.label: Post-fall huddle: what would you change?

options.label: Call light clipped within her reach, bed low and locked, nonslip socks, night light, floor kept dry, toileting rounds before 06:00
Raise all the bed rails and ask for a restraint at night

source.note: The nurse reaches the room about 2 min after the call light and a shout. No published standard was found for this interval.

then.log: The nurse arrives and kneels beside her. "Don't move, Mrs. Lindqvist. Tell me what you found."

source.note: Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Left alone without being told to stay still, she tries to get up after about a minute.

then.log: Alone, she grabs the bed rail and tries to stand. Her right leg gives way and she falls again.

source.note: If nobody calls, the nurse comes past on her 06:25 round.

then.log: The nurse comes past on her round and finds you both. "Why didn't you call me?"

source.note: The nurse's head-to-toe check on the floor takes about 3 min. No published standard was found for this interval.

then.log: Nurse: "Possible right hip fracture, and she hit her head on a blood thinner. I'm calling the provider and 911. Take a full set of vital signs and tell me, then stay with her: keep her still and warm and call me the moment anything changes." She steps out to the phone.

source.note: Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. New drowsiness and repeated questions about 6 min after the nurse's assessment. FLAG: the timing of a change after a head injury varies from minutes to hours; this is chosen to fall inside the run.

then.log: Mrs. Lindqvist asks what happened, then asks again. Her eyes keep closing.

source.note: Paramedics arrive about 20 min after the nurse calls 911. No published standard was found for this interval.

then.log: Paramedics arrive, splint her leg and move her onto the stretcher with the team. She leaves for the hospital.

triggers.when: live and t >= promptAt and not nurseHere and not away and not movedHer

effects.log: "Just help me up, dear. I'm fine, really." She reaches for your arm.

helpMeUp.title: "Help me up, dear"
helpMeUp.context: She is reaching for your arm and starting to push herself up.

choices.label: Help her up: she says she's fine

effects.log: As you lift, she screams and her right leg gives way. You lower her back to the floor.

choices.feedback: Moving her before the nurse checks her can turn a hip fracture into a worse one.

choices.label: "Please stay still; the nurse is coming to check you. I'm staying right here."

effects.log: She sighs and lies back. "All right."

choices.feedback: Don't move a resident after a fall until the nurse has checked her.

choices.label: Get the mechanical lift and do it yourself

effects.log: A lift needs two staff and the nurse's check first. You stay.

choices.feedback: A lift is how she will get up, but only after the nurse's check and with two people.

firstMoves.question: You have found Mrs. Lindqvist on the floor. What do you do first, and what will you tell the nurse?

parts.label: First moves
parts.criteria: Does not move her or help her up; calls for the nurse without leaving her (call light, calling out); tells her to stay still and reassures her; keeps her warm and covers bleeding with gentle pressure; observes. Stays within the aide's role (no assessment conclusions, no medications).
parts.modelAnswer: Leave her where she is and don't help her up. Press the call light and call out for the nurse while I stay with her. Tell her to stay still, cover her with a blanket and put gentle pressure on the skin tear with gloves on. Watch how alert she is and how she is breathing.

parts.label: What to tell the nurse
parts.criteria: Reports in objective words: when and where she was found and her position, her own words (wet floor, right hip pain about 7, hit her head), what is seen (right leg shorter and turned out, forehead bump, skin tear), the care plan's blood-thinner flag, and any change, without diagnosing.
parts.modelAnswer: Found at 06:10 on her right side beside the bed. She said she needed the bathroom, the floor was wet, her right hip hurts about a 7 and she thinks she hit her head. Her right leg looks shorter and turned out, there is a bump on her forehead and a skin tear on her right forearm. Her care plan says she is on a blood thinner.

noProgress.rationale: She reached the hospital safely, but without the aide's note and huddle input the facility loses what happened and how to prevent the next fall; a gap, not harm in itself.

Written for hospitals; the same universal precautions are applied here in a nursing home.

moved.label: Moved before she was checked
moved.narrative: She was moved, or got up, before the nurse checked her. The x-ray at the hospital shows a displaced hip fracture, which now needs a bigger operation.

safeHandoff.label: Kept still, help called, change reported, handed over

handoffGaps.label: Handed over, with gaps
handoffGaps.narrative: She reached the hospital without being moved, but something was late or missing: the call for help, the report, the vital signs, the change in her alertness, or the note.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written reasoning: first moves and the report

kpis.label: Change in alertness to telling the nurse

expertPath.text: Don't move her. Press the call light and call out for the nurse, staying with her. Tell her to stay still.
Ask what happened and look her over without moving her: right leg shorter and turned out, forehead bump, skin tear. Blanket on; gloves and gentle pressure on the skin tear.
She asks to be helped up: no, the nurse is coming to check her.
Nurse arrives: report the time and position, her words, what you saw and the blood-thinner flag.
Vital signs without moving her, told to the nurse. Stay, keep her still and warm, and watch.
Drowsy and repeating questions: call the nurse back at once.
Paramedics take her. Write an objective note; at the huddle suggest the universal fall precautions she was missing.

safeHandoff.headline: Kept still, help called, change reported, handed over
safeHandoff.body: You left her where she was, got the nurse without leaving, reported in objective words and caught the change in her alertness. That is the expert path.

handoffGaps.headline: Handed over, with gaps
handoffGaps.body: She was not moved, which mattered most. Look at what was late or missing: the call, the report, the vital signs, the change in her alertness, or the note.

moved.headline: Moved before she was checked
moved.body: The most useful kind of run to learn from. A resident on the floor stays on the floor until the nurse has checked her, however much she asks; the lift and the team get her up.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: The hour ran out before the note and the huddle were done.

scoring.modelReasoning: A resident found on the floor stays there until the nurse has checked her: possible hip fracture (a right leg shorter and turned out) and a head bump on a blood thinner. The aide calls the nurse at once without leaving (call light, calling out), tells her to stay still and stays, keeps her warm, puts gentle pressure on the skin tear, and observes. To the nurse: when and where she was found, her own words, what is seen, and the care plan's blood-thinner flag, in objective words. Vital signs without moving her when asked (pulse above 100 is reported). A new change in alertness is told to the nurse at once. Afterward: an objective note, and the universal fall precautions she was missing (call light in reach, bed low, nonslip socks, light, dry floor, toileting rounds), not rails or restraints.

whyNotUp.ask: While the nurse is on the way: she says she's fine. Why not just help her up?

choices.label: She may have a fracture or head injury; the nurse checks before anyone moves her
It's fine if she says she is fine

whyNotUp.explain: After a fall, don't move the resident unless she is in immediate danger, and tell the nurse at once so she can be assessed. When it is time, a mechanical lift and the team raise her from the floor.

source.cite: Chippewa Valley Technical College, Nursing Assistant (Open RN, CC BY 4.0), 3.2 Emergency Situations
source.note: Read 2026-11-10: after a fall, 'do not move them unless they are in immediate danger of further injury'; 'Notify the nurse as soon as you observe the situation so the resident can be assessed and treated'; a mechanical lift is typically used to raise the resident from the floor.

hipSign.ask: Her right leg looks shorter than the left and turned outward. What could that mean?

choices.label: A cramp from lying on the floor

hipSign.explain: A shortened, outward-turned leg is the classic picture of a hip fracture. The aide reports what is seen; the nurse and provider decide what it is.

source.note: Read 2026-11-10: 'The classically described presentation is a shortened and externally rotated limb.'

headThinner.ask: She hit her head and her care plan says blood thinner. Why does that change what you watch for?

choices.label: Bleeding inside the head is more likely and can show up later, so any change is reported at once
It doesn't; a bump is a bump

headThinner.explain: People on anticoagulants who hit their head are watched closely: UK guidance suggests considering a head scan within 8 hours even without other signs. For the aide that means watching alertness and telling the nurse the moment anything changes.
